newsitem.title: USA: Slow decline seen in U.S. cigarette consumption.
newsitem.headline: Slow decline seen in U.S. cigarette consumption.

text.p: U.S. cigarette manufacturers are likely to face a continued slow decline in domestic consumption over the next few years, but exports should grow, a government economist said.

"For the next few years, domestic cigarette consumption is likely to decline slowly ... mostly due to higher taxes and greater restrictions on where people can smoke," Tom Capehart of the Agriculture Department said in papers issued at the agency's annual agricultural outlook forum.

He said the major challenges to manufacturers in the final third of the decade would be from litigation and Food and Drug Administration regulation. Twenty-two state attorneys general have sued the tobacco industry seeking to recoup medicaid costs.
Twenty-five percent of Americans smoke cigarettes, currently consuming 487 billion a year.
Exports were expected to continue to rise through the end of the decade.
"Effective publicity campaigns worldwide have generated strong demand for U.S. cigarette brands," Capehart said.

The United States manufactured 750 billion cigarettes in 1996, 1 percent more than the previous year, while U.S. growers prdouced 1.6 billion pounds of tobacco (0.7 million metric tons), valued at an estimated $2.7 billion.
China was by far the world's leading leaf producer last year with output of around 55 billion pounds (2.5 million metric tons).

Several official Chinese sources have reported a rise in antismoking activities and a subsequent decline in smoking, Peter Burr, of the Agriculture Department's Foreign Agricultural Service said in papers issued at the forum.

"Other reports from Beijing and Shanghai do not support this. ... Cigarette production is projected to increase approximately 2 percent in 1997," he said. Burr estimated that in Beijing 60 percent of men 20 to 40 years old smoke.
